title: Strings
text:
Creating a string

string1 <- "This is a sting"

string2 <- 'Include "quote" with single quotes'


Escapes

double_quote <- "\"" # or '"'
single_quote <- "\'" # or "'"
backslash <- "\\"

# can see content with str_view()
x <- c(double_quote, single_quote, backslash)
str_view(x)

[1] │ "
[2] │ '
[3] │ \




Raw strings

tricky <- "double_quote <- \"\\\"\" # or '\"' single_quote <- '\\'' # or \"'\""
str_view(tricky)

[1] │ double_quote <- "\"" # or '"' single_quote <- '\'' # or "'"

# Use raw string 
tricky <- r"(double_quote <- "\"" # or '"' single_quote <- '\'' # or "'")"
str_view(tricky)

[1] │ double_quote <- "\"" # or '"' single_quote <- '\'' # or "'"




Other special characters
Most common: \n (new line) and \t (tab). See complete list under ?Quotes.

x <- c("one\ntwo", "one\ttwo", "\u00b5", "\U0001f604")
x

[1] "one\ntwo" "one\ttwo" "µ"        "😄"      

str_view(x)

[1] │ one
    │ two
[2] │ one{\t}two
[3] │ µ
[4] │ 😄

title: Strings
text:
Creating many strings from data

str_c()
Takes any number of vectors as arguments and returns a character vector:

str_c("x", "y")

[1] "xy"

str_c("x", "y", "z", sep = " ")

[1] "x y z"

str_c("Hello ", c("John", "Susan"))

[1] "Hello John"  "Hello Susan"


Documentation: str_c() similar to paste0() - BUT designed to be used with mutate():

df <- tibble(name = c("Flora", "David", "Terra", NA))

df |> mutate(greeting = str_c("Hi ", name, "!"))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  name  greeting 
  <chr> <chr>    
1 Flora Hi Flora!
2 David Hi David!
3 Terra Hi Terra!
4 <NA>  <NA>     


Missing values can be displayed in another way using coalesce() to replace them:

# Documentation 'Value' - Vector with same type and size
df |>
  mutate(
    greeting1 = str_c("Hi ", coalesce(name, "you"), "!"),
    greeting2 = coalesce(str_c("Hi ", name, "!"), "Hi!")
  )

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  name  greeting1 greeting2
  <chr> <chr>     <chr>    
1 Flora Hi Flora! Hi Flora!
2 David Hi David! Hi David!
3 Terra Hi Terra! Hi Terra!
4 <NA>  Hi you!   Hi!      




str_glue()
Mixing many fixed and variable strings with str_c() requires typing a lot of "s. Alternative: Use glue package via str_glue() - special feature: Anything inside {} will be evaluated like it’s outside of quotes (see ?str_glue):

df |>
  mutate(greeting = str_glue("Hi {name}"))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  name  greeting
  <chr> <glue>  
1 Flora Hi Flora
2 David Hi David
3 Terra Hi Terra
4 <NA>  Hi NA   




str_flatten()
str_flatten() works with summarize() - takes character vector and combines each element of the vector into single string:

str_flatten(c("x", "y", "z"))

[1] "xyz"

str_flatten(c("x", "y", "z"), collapse = ", ")

[1] "x, y, z"

str_flatten(c("x", "y", "z"), collapse = ", ", last = ", and ")

[1] "x, y, and z"

# Works well with summarize:

df <- tribble(
  ~ name, ~ fruit,
  "Carmen", "banana",
  "Carmen", "apple",
  "Marvin", "nectarine",
  "Terence", "cantaloupe",
  "Terence", "papaya",
  "Terence", "mandarin"
)

df |> 
  group_by(name) |>
  summarize(fruits = str_flatten(fruit, collapse = ", "))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  name    fruits                      
  <chr>   <chr>                       
1 Carmen  banana, apple               
2 Marvin  nectarine                   
3 Terence cantaloupe, papaya, mandarin

title: Strings
text:
Extracting data from strings
Common that multiple variables getting crammed together into a single string.
Four different tidyr functions for extraction: + df |> separate_longer_delim(col, delim) + df |> separate_longer_position(col, width) + df |> separate_wider_delim(col, delim, names) + `df |> separate_wider_position(col, widths)```
Similar with pivot_longer() and pivot_wider() - make input data frame longer creating new rows and wider by generating new columns.
delim splits up string with delimiter like ", " or " ".; position splits at specific widths, like c(3, 5, 2).

Separating into rows
Useful when number of components varies from row to row. Most common case is splitting based on delimiter:

df1 <- tibble(x = c("a,b,c", "d,e", "f"))

df1 |>
  separate_longer_delim(x, delim = ",")

# A tibble: 6 × 1
  x    
  <chr>
1 a    
2 b    
3 c    
4 d    
5 e    
6 f    

df2 <- tibble(x = c("1211", "131", "21"))

df2 |>
  separate_longer_position(x, width = 1)

# A tibble: 9 × 1
  x    
  <chr>
1 1    
2 2    
3 1    
4 1    
5 1    
6 3    
7 1    
8 2    
9 1    




Separating into columns
Useful when fixed numbers of components in each string, and want to spread into columns:

df3 <- tibble(x = c("a10.1.2022", "b10.2.2011", "e15.1.2015"))

df3 |>
  separate_wider_delim(x,
                       delim = ".",
                       names = c("code", "edition", "year")
                       )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  code  edition year 
  <chr> <chr>   <chr>
1 a10   1       2022 
2 b10   2       2011 
3 e15   1       2015 

# Can also omit specific piece by NA

df3 |>
  separate_wider_delim(x,
                       delim = ".",
                       names = c("code", NA, "year")
                       )

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  code  year 
  <chr> <chr>
1 a10   2022 
2 b10   2011 
3 e15   2015 

# separate_wider_position() needs specifying width of each column

df4 <- tibble(x = c("202215TX", "202122LA", "202325CA"))

df4 |>
  separate_wider_position(
    x,
    widths = c(year = 4, age = 2, state = 2)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  year  age   state
  <chr> <chr> <chr>
1 2022  15    TX   
2 2021  22    LA   
3 2023  25    CA

#  separate_wider_delim(
#    a,
#    delim = "-",
#    names = c("x", "y", "z")
#  )

 df |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    a, delim = "-", names = c("x","y","z"),
    too_few = "debug"
  )

`a_remainder`.

Subsetting
Extract parts of string via str_sub(string, start, end). + start and end are position where substring starts and ends (inclusive arguments). Length of returned string: end - start + 1:

x <- c("Apple", "Banana", "Pear")

str_sub(x, start = 1, end = 3)

[1] "App" "Ban" "Pea"

# Can use negative values to count back from the end of the string:
# -1 is last character, -2 is second to last character

str_sub(x, start = -3, end = -1)

[1] "ple" "ana" "ear"

# Too short string; str_sub returns as much as possible

str_sub("a", start = -3, end = -1)

title: Strings
text:
Non-English text

Encoding
Underlying representation of strings in R accessed via charToRaw():

charToRaw("Hadley")

[1] 48 61 64 6c 65 79

# Each represents one letter
# mapping from hexadecimal numbers to character is called encoding
# Encoding is ASCII

For more read http://kunststube.net/encoding/.


Letter variations

u <- c("\u00fc", "u\u0308")
str_view(u)

[1] │ ü
[2] │ ü

str_length(u)

[1] 1 2

str_sub(u, 1, 1)

[1] "ü" "u"

u[[1]] == u[[2]]

[1] FALSE

str_equal(u[[1]], u[[2]])

[1] TRUE

title: Numbers
text:
Making numbers
Most cases, numbers will be recorded in R’s numeric type: integer or double. Sometimes as strings. readr provides useful functions parsing strings into numbers: parse_double() and parse_number().
Use parse_double() when numbers have been written as strings:

x <- c("1.2", "5.6", "1e3")
class(x)

[1] "character"

parse_double(x)

[1]    1.2    5.6 1000.0

class(parse_double(x))

[1] "numeric"


Use parse_number() when strings contain non-numeric text that we want to ignore. Useful for currency data and percentages:

x <- c("$1,234", "USD 3,513", "59%")
class(x)

[1] "character"

parse_number(x)

[1] 1234 3513   59

class(parse_number(x))

[1] "numeric"

text:
Numeric transformations
Transformation function work well with mutate() - as output is same length as input. Most transformation functions built in base R - will list only most practical one.

Arithmetic and recycling rules
Basics of arithmetic (x, -, *, /, ^). Recycling rules determine what happens with different size sides.
\(\rightarrow\) R handles mismatched lengths by recycling (repeating) the short vector:

x <- c(1, 2, 10, 20)
x / 5

[1] 0.2 0.4 2.0 4.0

# is shorthand for:
x / c(5, 5, 5, 5)

[1] 0.2 0.4 2.0 4.0


Want to recycle single numbers - BUT R will recylce any shorter length vector:

x * c(1, 2)

[1]  1  4 10 40

x * c(1, 2, 3)

Warning in x * c(1, 2, 3): longer object length is not a multiple of shorter
object length


[1]  1  4 30 20

I.e. division that yields a whole number and a remainder.
%/% = integer division %% = computes remainder

Logarithms
Used when dealing with data ranging across multiple orders and converting exponetial growth to linear growth.
Three choices: log(), log2()(base 2), log10()(base 10).
Inverse of log() is exp().


Rounding
round(x)round number to nearest integer.

round(123.456)

[1] 123


Can control precision of rounding with second argument, digits, i.e. round(x, digits).

round(123.456, digits = 2)

[1] 123.46

General transformations

Ranks
See documentation for: dplyr::min_rank(), dplyr::row_number(), dplyr::dense_rank()

[1]  1  2  3  4  5 NA

# equivalent to
rank(x, ties.method = "first", na.last = "keep") # see documentation

[1]  1  2  3  4  5 NA

min_rank(desc(x)) # largest values get smallest rank

[1]  5  3  3  2  1 NA

# Example with df

df |>
  mutate(
    row_number = row_number(x),
    dense_rank = dense_rank(x),

title: Numbers
text:
Numeric summaries

Center
Alternativ to mean() is function median() - finding values in middle of vector.
For symmetric distribution, rather report mean, for skewed distributions usually report median.

flights |>
  group_by(year, month, day) |>
  summarize(
    mean = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x = mean, y = median)
  ) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point()










Minimum, maximum, and quantiles
Other locations: + min(), max() - giving largest and smallest values. + quantile() - Syntax: quantile(x, 0.25), finds x greater than 25% of the values. Note: median(x) == quantile(x, 0.5).

  group_by(year, month, day) |>
  summarize(

text:
Summaries

Logical summaries
Two main logical summaries: any() and all().
any(x) is equivalent to | \(\rightarrow\) returns TRUE if there any TRUE’s in x.
all(x) is equivalent to & \(\rightarrow\) returns TRUE if all values of x are TRUE.
Most summary function include na.rm = TRUE.

flights |>
  group_by(year, month, day) |>
  summarize(
    all_delayed = all(dep_delay <= 60, na.rm = TRUE), 
    any_long_delay = any(arr_delay >= 300, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Numeric summaries of logical vectors
Logical vectors is numeric context, TRUE becomes 1, FALSE becomes 0 \(\rightarrow\) sum() and mean() useful with logical vectors:

sum(x): gives number of TRUEs
mean(x): gives proportion of TRUEs


flights |> 
  group_by(year, month, day) |>
  summarize(
    proportion_delayed = mean(dep_delay <= 60, na.rm = TRUE),
    count_long_delay = sum(arr_delay >= 300, na.rm = TRUE), 
    .groups = "drop"

Logical subsetting
Can use logical vector to filter single variable to a subset of interest:

# Avg. delay of flights, that were actually delayed
flights |>
  filter(arr_delay > 0) |>
  group_by(year, month, day) |>
  summarize(
    behind = mean(arr_delay),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

    year month   day behind     n

# How to also compute avg. delay for flights arriving early?
# Use inline filtering with [
flights |>
  group_by(year, month, day) |>
  summarize(
    behind = mean(arr_delay[arr_delay > 0], na.rm = TRUE),
    ahead = mean(arr_delay[arr_delay < 0], na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# A tibble: 365 × 6
    year month   day behind ahead     n

10  2013     1    10   27.3 -16.4   932

# Note: n() now return total number of flights



Conditional transformation
Two important tools: if_else() and case_when().

if_else()






Note



Main advantage to base R’s ìfelse() is that with dyplr::if_else() can choose what happens to missing values, and it’s more likely to give meaningful error when variable types not compatible.


Format: if_else(condition, true, false, missing)

x <- c(-3:3, NA)
if_else(x > 0, "+ve", "-ve")

[1] "-ve" "-ve" "-ve" "-ve" "+ve" "+ve" "+ve" NA   

# How to deal with NA
if_else(x > 0, "+ve", "-ve", "???")

[1] "-ve" "-ve" "-ve" "-ve" "+ve" "+ve" "+ve" "???"

# can also use vectors for true and false
if_else(x > 0, -x, x)

[1] -3 -2 -1  0 -1 -2 -3 NA

# Can also implement simple coalesce() version
x1 <- c(NA, 1, 2, NA)
y1 <- c(3, NA, 4, 6)
if_else(is.na(x1), y1, x1) # replacing NA values

[1] 3 1 2 6

# Can also nest if_else() in if_else()
if_else(x == 0, "0", if_else(x < 0, "-ve", "+ve"), "?")

[1] "-ve" "-ve" "-ve" "0"   "+ve" "+ve" "+ve" "?"  








Tip



With more conditions, switch to dyplr::case_when().





case_when()
Different computations for different conditions. Syntax: condition ~ output. condition must be a logical vector - when TRUE, output will be used:

case_when(
  x == 0 ~ "0",
  x > 0 ~ "+ve",
  x < 0 ~ "-ve",
  is.na(x) ~ "???"
)

[1] "-ve" "-ve" "-ve" "0"   "+ve" "+ve" "+ve" "???"

# Can also specify default for all other values:
case_when(
  x < 0 ~ "-ve",
  x > 0 ~ "+ve",
  .default = "???"
)

[1] "-ve" "-ve" "-ve" "???" "+ve" "+ve" "+ve" "???"

# Note: if multiple conditions match, only first will be used:
case_when(
  x > 0 ~ "+ve",
  x > 2 ~ "big"
)

[1] NA    NA    NA    NA    "+ve" "+ve" "+ve" NA   


Can also use variables on both sides of ~; can mix and match variables as needed.

flights |>
  mutate(
    status = case_when(
      is.na(arr_delay) ~ "cancelled",
      arr_delay < -30 ~ "very early",
      arr_delay < -15 ~ "early",
      abs(arr_delay) <= 15 ~ "on time",
      arr_delay < 60 ~ "late",
      arr_delay < Inf ~ "very late"
    ),
    .keep = "used"
  )

# A tibble: 336,776 × 2
   arr_delay status 
       <dbl> <chr>  
 1        11 on time
 2        20 late   
 3        33 late   
 4       -18 early  
 5       -25 early  
 6        12 on time
 7        19 late   
 8       -14 on time
 9        -8 on time
10         8 on time
# ℹ 336,766 more rows




Compatible types
if_else() and case_when() require compatible types in output:

Numerical and logical vectors are compatible
strings and factors are compatible
Dates and date-times are compatible
NA is compatible with everything

title: dates-and-times
text:
Creating date/times
Three types of date/time data refering to instant in time:

date: Tibbles print this as <date>
time within day: Tibbles print this as <time>
date-time date plus time: Uniquely identifies instant in time. Tibbles print this as  - Base R calls these POSIXct







Tip



Use simplest possible data type - if can work with date instead of date-time, then do.



# Current time and date
today()

[1] "2026-07-26"

now()

[1] "2026-07-26 18:32:26 CEST"



During import
CSV contains ISO8601 date or date-time - readr will automatically recognize it:

csv <- "
date,datetime
2022-01-02, 2022-01-02 05:12
"
read_csv(file = csv)

Warning: The `file` argument of `read_csv()` should use `I()` for literal data as of
readr 2.2.0.
  
  # Bad (for example):
  read_csv("x,y\n1,2")
  
  # Good:
  read_csv(I("x,y\n1,2"))


Rows: 1 Columns: 2
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
dttm (1): datetime
date (1): date

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.


# A tibble: 1 × 2
  date       datetime           
  <date>     <dttm>             
1 2022-01-02 2022-01-02 05:12:00








Note



ISO8601 - international standard for writing dates - e.g., May 3 2022 is 2022-05-03. Can include time separated by :. Date and time separated either by space or T - 2022-05-03 16:26 or 2022-05-03T16:26.


Other date-time formats require use of col_types plus col_date() or col_datetime() with date-time format. See ?col_date for all format specifications! - e.g., %Y-%m-%d specifies a date that’s a year, -, month (as number) -, day:

csv <- "
  date
  01/02/15
"

read_csv(
  file = csv,
  col_types = cols(
    date = col_date(format = "%d/%m/%y")
  )
)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  date      
  <date>    
1 2015-02-01

read_csv(
  file = csv,
  col_types = cols(
    date = col_date(format = "%m/%d/%y")
  )
)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  date      
  <date>    
1 2015-01-02

read_csv(
  file = csv,
  col_types = cols(
    date = col_date(format = "%y/%m/%d")
  )
)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  date      
  <date>    
1 2001-02-15


Using %b or %B needs locale() - see date_names_langs() or create via date_names().


From strings
Lubridate’s helpers attempt to determine formate once order is specified - then lubridate function will parse the date:

ymd("2017-01-31")

[1] "2017-01-31"

# str_view(ymd("2017-01-31"))
# class(ymd("2017-01-31"))

mdy("January 1st, 2017")

[1] "2017-01-01"

dmy("31-Jan-2017")

[1] "2017-01-31"


ymd() and friends create date. Creating date-time needs underscore and “h”, “m”, “s” to name of parsing function:

ymd_hms("2017-01-31 20:11:59")

[1] "2017-01-31 20:11:59 UTC"

mdy_hm("01/31/2017 08:01")

[1] "2017-01-31 08:01:00 UTC"

# Can also force creatiom of date-time by spplying time zone:
ymd("2017-01-31", tz = "UTC")

[1] "2017-01-31 UTC"




From individual components
Date-time components across multiple columns - use make_date() for date, make_datetime() for date-times:

flights |>
  select(year, month, day, hour, minute)

# A tibble: 336,776 × 5
    year month   day  hour minute
   <int> <int> <int> <dbl>  <dbl>
 1  2013     1     1     5     15
 2  2013     1     1     5     29
 3  2013     1     1     5     40
 4  2013     1     1     5     45
 5  2013     1     1     6      0
 6  2013     1     1     5     58
 7  2013     1     1     6      0
 8  2013     1     1     6      0
 9  2013     1     1     6      0
10  2013     1     1     6      0
# ℹ 336,766 more rows

flights |>
  select(year, month, day, hour, minute) |>
  mutate(date = make_date(year = year,
                          month = month,
                          day = day),
         departure = make_datetime(year = year,
                                  month = month,
                                  day = day,
                                  hour = hour,
                                  min = minute)
         )

# A tibble: 336,776 × 7
    year month   day  hour minute date       departure          
   <int> <int> <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <date>     <dttm>             
 1  2013     1     1     5     15 2013-01-01 2013-01-01 05:15:00
 2  2013     1     1     5     29 2013-01-01 2013-01-01 05:29:00
 3  2013     1     1     5     40 2013-01-01 2013-01-01 05:40:00
 4  2013     1     1     5     45 2013-01-01 2013-01-01 05:45:00
 5  2013     1     1     6      0 2013-01-01 2013-01-01 06:00:00
 6  2013     1     1     5     58 2013-01-01 2013-01-01 05:58:00
 7  2013     1     1     6      0 2013-01-01 2013-01-01 06:00:00
 8  2013     1     1     6      0 2013-01-01 2013-01-01 06:00:00
 9  2013     1     1     6      0 2013-01-01 2013-01-01 06:00:00
10  2013     1     1     6      0 2013-01-01 2013-01-01 06:00:00
# ℹ 336,766 more rows


Can do same thing with the four time columns in flights: dep_time, sched_dep_time, arr_time, sched_arr_time:

make_dttm <- function(year, month, day, time){
  make_datetime(year, month, day, time %/% 100, time %% 100)
}

flights_dt <- flights |>
  filter(!is.na(dep_time), !is.na(arr_time)) |>
  mutate(
    dep_time = make_dttm(year, month, day, dep_time),
    sched_dep_time = make_dttm(year, month, day, sched_dep_time),
    arr_time = make_dttm(year, month, day, arr_time),
    sched_arr_time = make_dttm(year, month, day, sched_arr_time)
  ) |>
  select(origin, dest, ends_with("delay"), ends_with("time"))

# Can visualize distribution of departure times across the year:

ggplot(
  data = flights_dt,
  mapping = aes(x = dep_time)
) +
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 86400) # 86400 seconds = 1 day







# within single day
flights_dt |>
  filter(dep_time < ymd(20130102)) |> # "2013-01-02" would work as well 
  ggplot(aes(x = dep_time)) +
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 600) # 600 s = 10 min














Note



After call make_datetime(), the variable is no longer stored as hours and minutes—it becomes a full datetime measured internally in seconds. E.g., dep_time is now a POSIXct datetime. Internally, R stores a POSIXct values as: the number of seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. See as.numeric(make_dttm(2013, 1, 1, 5, 17)) will return large number which is seconds since 1970. For dates, 1 means 1 day; for date-time, 1 means 1 second.




From other types
Switching between date-time and date via as_datetime() and as_date()

# from date to date-time
today()

[1] "2026-07-26"

as_datetime(today())

[1] "2026-07-26 UTC"

# from date-time to date
now()

[1] "2026-07-26 18:32:28 CEST"

as_date(now())

[1] "2026-07-26"

text:
Date-time components
You can pull out individual parts of the date with the accessor functions year(), month(), mday() (day of the month), yday() (day of the year), wday() (day of the week), hour(), minute(), and second(). These are effectively the opposites of make_datetime().

datetime <- ymd_hms("2026-07-08 12:34:56 ")

year(datetime)

[1] 2026

month(datetime, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE) # optional arguments displayed

[1] July
12 Levels: January < February < March < April < May < June < ... < December

day(datetime)

[1] 8

hour(datetime)

[1] 12

minute(datetime)

[1] 34

second(datetime)

[1] 56

mday(datetime)

[1] 8

yday(datetime)

[1] 189

wday(datetime, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE) # optional arguments displayed

[1] Wednesday
7 Levels: Sunday < Monday < Tuesday < Wednesday < Thursday < ... < Saturday



# Example: On what day most flights?
flights_dt |>
  mutate(wday = wday(dep_time, label =TRUE)) |>
  count(wday)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  wday      n
  <ord> <int>
1 Sun   45583
2 Mon   49396
3 Tue   49226
4 Wed   48753
5 Thu   48565
6 Fri   48645
7 Sat   37895

flights_dt |>
  mutate(wday = wday(dep_time, label =TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = wday)) +
  geom_bar()







# Example: Average departure delay by minute
flights_dt |>
  mutate(minute = minute(dep_time)) |>
  group_by(minute) |>
  summarize(
    avg_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x = minute, y = avg_delay)
  ) +
  geom_line()







flights_dt |>
  mutate(minute = minute(sched_dep_time)) |>
  group_by(minute) |>
  summarize(
    avg_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x = minute, y = avg_delay)
  ) +
  geom_line()









Rounding
Plotting individual components by rounding the date to nearby unit of time - floor_date(), round_date(), ceiling_date() - takes vector of dates to adjust and name of unit to round:

# Number of flights per week
flights_dt |>
  count(week = floor_date(dep_time, unit = "week")) |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = week, y = n)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()







# Distribution of flights across course of day; dep_time - earliest instance of thst day:

flights_dt |>
  mutate(dep_hour = dep_time - floor_date(dep_time, unit = "day")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = dep_hour)) +
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 60 * 30)

Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type <difftime>.
Defaulting to continuous.








flights_dt |>
  mutate(dep_hour = hms::as_hms(dep_time - floor_date(dep_time, unit = "day"))) |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = dep_hour)) +
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 60 * 30)










Modifying components
Can use accessor functions to modify components of a date/time. Useful when cleaning data that has incorrect dates:

(datetime <- ymd_hms("2026-07-08 12:34:56"))

[1] "2026-07-08 12:34:56 UTC"

year(datetime) <- 2030

month(datetime) <- 01

hour(datetime) <- hour(datetime) + 1
datetime

[1] "2030-01-08 13:34:56 UTC"

# Alterntively use update():

update(datetime, year = 2030, month = 01, mday = 2, hour = 2)

[1] "2030-01-02 02:34:56 UTC"

# Big values cause "roll-over"
update(ymd("2023-02-01"), mday = 30)

[1] "2023-03-02"




Exercises

# Exercise1: How does distribution of flights within day change over course of year?
flights_dt |>
  filter(!is.na(dep_time)) |>
  mutate(dep_hour = update(dep_time, yday = 1)) |>
  mutate(month = factor(month(dep_time))) |>
  ggplot(aes(dep_hour, color = month)) +
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 60 * 60)

flights_dt |>
  mutate(dep_delay0 = as.numeric(dep_time - sched_dep_time) / 60) |>
  filter(!is.na(dep_delay)) |>
  mutate(diff = dep_delay - dep_delay0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_freqpoly()

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.

flights_dt |>
  filter(!is.na(dep_time), !is.na(arr_time), !is.na(air_time)) |>
  mutate(
    duration = as.numeric(arr_time - dep_time) / 60,
    diff = duration - air_time
  ) |>
  group_by(origin, dest) |>
  summarize(
    avg_duration = mean(duration),
    avg_air_time = mean(air_time),
    avg_diff = mean(diff),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(avg_diff)

  mutate(sched_dep_hour = hour(sched_dep_time)) |>

title: dates-and-times
text:
Time spans
Arithmetic with dates - subtraction, addition, division.
Three important classes representing time spans:

Durations - represent exact number of seconds
Periods - represents human units like weeks and months
Intervals - represent a starting and ending point


Durations
In R when subtracting two dates, we get difftime object:

h_age <- today() - ymd("2004-03-22")
h_age

Time difference of 8161 days


difftime class object record a time span of seconds, minutes, hours, days, or weeks. Ambiguity problematic - lubridate provides alternative which always uses seconds: the duration:

as.duration(h_age)

[1] "705110400s (~22.34 years)"

class(h_age)

[1] "difftime"



# Different duration constructors
dseconds(15)

[1] "15s"

dminutes(10)

[1] "600s (~10 minutes)"

dhours(c(12, 24))

[1] "43200s (~12 hours)" "86400s (~1 days)"  

ddays(0:5)

[1] "0s"                "86400s (~1 days)"  "172800s (~2 days)"
[4] "259200s (~3 days)" "345600s (~4 days)" "432000s (~5 days)"

dweeks(3)

[1] "1814400s (~3 weeks)"

dyears(1)

[1] "31557600s (~1 years)"


Durations always convert time span in seconds.

# Add and multiple durations:
2 * dyears(1)

[1] "63115200s (~2 years)"

dyears(1) + dweeks(12) + dhours(15)

[1] "38869200s (~1.23 years)"

# Add and subtract durations to and from days:
tomorrow <- today() + ddays(1)
tomorrow

[1] "2026-07-27"

last_year <- today() - dyears(1)
last_year

[1] "2025-07-25 18:00:00 UTC"




Periods
Are time spans but don’t have fixed length in seconds - work with “human” times, like days and months:

one_am <- ymd_hms("2026-03-08 01:00:00", tz = "America/New_York")

one_am

[1] "2026-03-08 01:00:00 EST"

one_am + days(1)

[1] "2026-03-09 01:00:00 EDT"


Periods can be created with constructor functions:

hours(c(12, 24))

[1] "12H 0M 0S" "24H 0M 0S"

days(7)

[1] "7d 0H 0M 0S"

months(1:6)

[1] "1m 0d 0H 0M 0S" "2m 0d 0H 0M 0S" "3m 0d 0H 0M 0S" "4m 0d 0H 0M 0S"
[5] "5m 0d 0H 0M 0S" "6m 0d 0H 0M 0S"

# Can add and multiply:
10 * (months(6) + days(1))

[1] "60m 10d 0H 0M 0S"

days(50) + hours(25) + minutes(2)

[1] "50d 25H 2M 0S"

# Adding to dates

ymd("2024-01-01") + dyears(1)

[1] "2024-12-31 06:00:00 UTC"

Time zones

title: Communication
text:
Goal: Communicating understandings to others
\(\rightarrow\) make plots as self-explanatory as possible

title: Communication
text:
Scales
Scales control how aesthetic mappings will be displayed

Default scales
ggplot2 automatically adds scales:

ggplot(
  data = mpg, 
  mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(color = class)
  )







# Behind the scenes
ggplot(
  data = mpg,
  mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy)
) + 
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(color = class)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous() + # puts values of displ on continuous line on x-axis
  scale_y_continuous() +
  scale_color_discrete() # chooses colors for each of the class of car








Scales are named according to type of variable:

continuous
discrete
datetime
date

Reasons to override defaults:

changing paramters of default scale, allowing e.g. to change breaks on axes, or key labels on the legend
replacing scales, and using different algorithm



Axis ticks and legend keys
Axis and legends are calles guides. Axis are used for x/y aesthetics; legends for everything else.
Two arguments affecting appearance of ticks on axis and keys on legend: breaks and labels:

break: controls position of ticks; - values associated with keys
labels: controls text labels


ggplot(
  data = mpg,
  mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)
) + 
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(from = 15, to = 40, by = 5))








Can use labels same way, or set NULL to suppress. For discrete scales for categorical variables, labels can be named list of existing level names and desired labels for them:

# Example: Rescaling and relabeling x-axis
ggplot(
  data = mpg,
  mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy)
) + 
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(from = 2, to = 7, length.out = 3),
    labels = c("A", "B", "C"))







# Example: labels = NULL
ggplot(
  data = mpg,
  mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)
) + 
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = NULL) +
  scale_color_discrete(labels = c(
    "4" = "4-wheel",
    "f" = "front",
    "r" = "rear"
  ))














Tip



labels coupled with labelling functions from scales package useful for formatting numbers as currency, percent, etc.



# Left
ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = price, y = cut)
) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.05) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar())







# Right
ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = price, y = cut)
) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.05) + 
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = label_dollar(scale = 1/1000, # divide dollar values by 1000
                          suffix = "K"), # add suffix
    breaks = seq(from = 1000, to = 19000, by = 6000) # add custom breaks
  )








Another label function is label_percent():

ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = cut, fill = clarity)
) +
   geom_bar(position = "fill") + # position = "fill" return proportions at every x-position; most useful for geoms anchored to x-axis, like geom_bar()
   scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(),
    name = "Percentage"
   )








Another use of breaks when having few data points, wanting to highlight where observations occur:

# Presidential dataset
glimpse(presidential)

Rows: 12
Columns: 4
$ name  <chr> "Eisenhower", "Kennedy", "Johnson", "Nixon", "Ford", "Carter", "…
$ start <date> 1953-01-20, 1961-01-20, 1963-11-22, 1969-01-20, 1974-08-09, 197…
$ end   <date> 1961-01-20, 1963-11-22, 1969-01-20, 1974-08-09, 1977-01-20, 198…
$ party <chr> "Republican", "Democratic", "Democratic", "Republican", "Republi…

presidential |>
  mutate(id = 33 + row_number()) |> # add id corresponding to number of pres.
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x = start, y = id)
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_segment(
    mapping = aes(xend = end, yend = id)
  ) +
  scale_x_date(name = NULL,
               breaks = presidential$start,
               date_labels = "'%y"
  )










Legend layout
Controls overall position of the legend using theme() setting - they control non-data parts of the plot. Theme setting legend.position controls where the legend is drawn:

base <- ggplot(
  data = mpg, 
  mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy)
) + 
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(color = class)
  )

base + theme(legend.position = "right") # default







base + theme(legend.position = "left")







base +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 3))







base +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 3))














Note



guides() along with guides_legend() or guide_colorbar() controls the display of individual legends. nrowcontrols number of rows the legend uses; override.aes overrides one of the aesthetics, e.g., making points bigger. Useful when used a low alphato display many points on a plot.



ggplot(
  data = mpg,
  mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy)
) + 
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(color = class)
  ) + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 3, override.aes = list(size= 4)))

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'















Note



Argument in guides() matches name of aesthetic, just like in labs().




Replacing a scale
Two types of scales likely to switch out: continuous position scales and color scales.

# Example - log transforming to better see relationship
# Left
ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = carat, y = price)
) + 
  geom_bin2d()

`stat_bin2d()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.








# Right
# Note: scales are labelled with transformed values
ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = log10(carat), y = log10(price))
) + 
  geom_bin2d()

`stat_bin2d()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.








# Instead doing transformation in aesthetic mapping, transform with scales
# Note: Scales are labelled with original values
ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = carat, y = price)
) + 
  geom_bin2d() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10()

`stat_bin2d()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.









Another scale frequently customized is color. Default categorical scale picks colors that are evenly spaced around the color wheel.
Useful alternative: ColorBrewer - tuned colors for color blindness.

ggplot(
  data = mpg,
  mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy)
) + 
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(color = drv)
  )







# For people with red-green color blindness: 
ggplot(
  data = mpg,
  mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(color = drv, shape = drv)
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") # See documentation for palettes














Tip



For ColorBrewer scales see online documentation at https://colorbrewer2.org/.


For predefined mapping, use scale_color_manual():

presidential |>
  mutate(id = 33 + row_number()) |>
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x = start, y = id, color = party)
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_segment(
    mapping = aes(yend = id, xend = end)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Name of president",
    breaks = seq(34, 45, by = 1),
    labels = presidential$name
    ) +
  scale_x_date(
    name = "Start of presidency",
    date_breaks = "4 years", # see documentation
    date_labels = "'%y"
    ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(Republican = "red", Democratic = "blue")
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top"
    ) +
  labs(
    title = "Presidential terms",
     color = "Party"
  )














Tip



For continuous color, use scale_color_gradient() or scale_fill_gradient(). For diverging scale use scale_color_gradient2() - allows to give negative and positive values different color.


One very useful color scale - viridis color scales:

df <- tibble(
  x = rnorm(10000),
  y =  rnorm(10000)
)

ggplot(
  data = df,
  mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)
) +
  geom_hex() +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(
    title = "Default, continous",
    x = NULL, 
    y = NULL
  )







ggplot(
  data = df, 
  mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)
) + 
  geom_hex() + 
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(
    title = "Viridius, continuous",
    x = NULL, 
    y = NULL
  )







ggplot(
  data = df, 
  mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)
) + 
  geom_hex() +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_fill_viridis_b() +
  labs(
    title = "Viridius, binned",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  )







ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_hex() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "red") +
  coord_fixed()














Note



Color scales come in two variables: scale_color_*() and scale_fill_*().




Zooming
Three ways to control plot limits:. 1. Adjust what data are plotted. 2. Set limits in each scale. 3. Set xlim and ylim in coord_cartesian()

# Left
ggplot(
  data = mpg, 
  mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(color = drv)
  ) +
  geom_smooth()

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'








# Right
mpg |> 
  filter(displ >= 5 & displ <= 6 & hwy >= 10 & hwy <= 25) |>
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy)
  ) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(color = drv)
  ) + 
  geom_smooth() + 
  scale_color_discrete(
    labels = c(
      "4" = "4-wheel",
      "f" = " front",
      "r" = "rear"
    )
  )

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'








# compare 'Right' to: 
ggplot(
  data = mpg, 
  mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(color = drv)
  ) +
  geom_smooth() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(5, 6), ylim = c(10, 25))

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'

title: Communication
text:
Themes
Customizing non-data elements of the plot with a theme:

ggplot(
  data = mpg, 
  mapping = aes(x = displ, y = hwy)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(color = drv)
  ) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  theme_bw()

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'















Note



ggplot includes 12 themes: *_bw(), *_light(), *_classic(), *_linedraw(), *_dark(), *_minimal(), *_gray(), *_void(); Many more in add-on packages like ggthemes.



ggplot(
  data = mpg, 
  mapping = aes(x= displ, y = hwy, color = drv)
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Larger engine sizes tend to have lower fuel economy",
    caption = "Source: https://fueleconomy.gov."
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.6, 0.7), # position of legend in plot
    legend.direction = "horizontal", # layout of items in legend
    legend.box.background = element_rect(color = "red"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 1),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "blue")
  )

title: Communication
text:
Layout
Patchwork package allows combining separate plots into same graphic:

p1 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Plot 1")
p2 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Plot 2")

p1 + p2 # First create and save both plots, then place next to each other with +







# Or more complex plot layout:
p3 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = cty, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Plot 3")

(p1 | p3) / p2








Patchwork allows collecting legends from multiple plots into one common legend - customizing placement, dimension, add title, subtitle, caption, etc. to the plots \(\rightarrow\) look through the guides on the package website: https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com.

title: The layered grammar of graphics
text:
Template
ggplot(data = <DATA>) +
  <GEOM_FUNCTION>(
    mapping = aes(<MAPPINGS>),
    stat = <STAT>,
    position = <POSITION>
  ) +
  <COORDINATE_FUNCTION> +
  <FACET_FUNCTION>






Important



The seven parameters in the template compose the grammar of graphics, a formal system for building plots. The grammar of graphics is based on the insight that you can uniquely describe any plot as a combination of a dataset, a geom, a set of mappings, a stat, a position adjustment, a coordinate system, a faceting scheme, and a theme.


Two very useful resources for getting an overview of the complete ggplot2 functionality are the ggplot2 cheatsheet (which can be found at https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets) and the ggplot2 package website (https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org).

Difference between geom_bar() and geom_col():

title: Exploratory data analysis - EDA
text:
Prerequisites

library(tidyverse)
library(ggthemes)

Goal: Develope understanding of the data by asking questions.
Key: To ask quality question one must first generate a large quantity of questions






Important



Two types of questions will always be useful for making discoveries within the data:

What type of variation occurs within my variables?
What type of covariation occurs between my variables?

title: Exploratory data analysis - EDA
text:
Variation
Variations is the tendency of the values of a variable to change from measurement to measurement. Each of measurement will include small amount of error that varies from measurement to measurement. Variables can also vary across different subjects or at different times. Every variable has own pattern of variation. Best way to understand that pattern is to visualize the distribution of the variable’s values

Diamond dataset

# ?diamonds
# str(diamonds)
diamonds
glimpse(diamonds)

Start by visualizing distribution of weights (carat) of ~54,000 diamonds from the diamonds dataset. caratis a numerical vairable, can use histogram:

ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = carat)
) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)










Typical values
In both, bar charts and histograms, tall bars show common values of a variable, and shorter bars show less-common values. Places with no bar, indicate that these values were not seen in the data. Look for anything unexpected:

Which values are the most common? Why?
Which values are rare? Why? Does this match our expectation?
Can we see any unusual pattern? What might explain them?

Distribution of carat for smaller diamonds:

smaller <- diamonds |>
  filter(carat < 3) |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = carat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.01)

print(smaller)








Questions:

Why are there more diamonds at whole carats and common fractions of carats?
Why are there more diamonds slightly to the right of each peak than there are slightly to the left of each peak?

Visualizations can also reveal clusters, which suggest existence of subgroups:

How are the observations within each subgroup similar to each other?
How are the observations in separate clusters different from each other?
How can you explain or describe the clusters?
Why might the appearance of clusters be misleading?



Unusual values
Outliers are observations that are unusual; Data points not fitting the pattern. Sometimes just data entry error, sometimes extreme values observed in data collection, sometimes they suggest important new findings
Sometimes, outliers are not easy to spot. E.g. take the distribution of the y variable from the diamonds dataset. The only evidence of outliers is the unusually wide limits on the x-axis.:

ggplot(
  data = diamonds, 
  mapping = aes(x = y)
) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)








Rare bins are very short, making it very difficult to see them. We need to zoom to small values of the y-axis with coord_cartesian():

ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = y)
) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 50))














Note



coord_cartesian() also has an xlim() argument for when you need to zoom into the x-axis. ggplot2 also has xlim() and ylim() functions that work slightly differently: they throw away the data outside the limits.


Can see and filter for the unusual items:

unusual <- diamonds |>
  filter(y < 3 | y > 20) |>
  select(price, x, y, z) |>
  arrange(y)

print(unusual)

# A tibble: 9 × 4
  price     x     y     z
  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  5139  0      0    0   
2  6381  0      0    0   
3 12800  0      0    0   
4 15686  0      0    0   
5 18034  0      0    0   
6  2130  0      0    0   
7  2130  0      0    0   
8  2075  5.15  31.8  5.12
9 12210  8.09  58.9  8.06








Note



The y variable measures one of the three dimensions of these diamonds, in mm. We know that diamonds can’t have a width of 0mm, so these values must be incorrect. By doing EDA, we have discovered missing data that was coded as 0, which we never would have found by simply searching for NAs. Going forward we might choose to re-code these values as NAs in order to prevent misleading calculations. We might also suspect that measurements of 32mm and 59mm are implausible: those diamonds are over an inch long, but don’t cost hundreds of thousands of dollars!




Unusual values
Two options when encountering unusual values in the dataset:

Drop entire row with strange values (not recommended):


diamonds2 <- diamonds |> 
  filter(between(y, 3, 20)) # between() as shortcut for x >= left & <= right; see ?between







Tip



?filter: These functions are used to subset a data frame, applying the expressions in … to determine which rows should be kept (for filter()) or dropped ( for filter_out()).



Replace unusual values with missing values (recommended): ::: {.callout-note} Easiest way is by mutate() to replace variable with modified copy. Can use ìf_else() function to replace values with NA: :::


diamonds2 <- diamonds |>
  mutate(y = ifelse(y < 3 | y > 20, NA, y))

Now, when plotting, ggplot will not include NA’s, but will warn!

ggplot(
  data = diamonds2,
  mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)
) + 
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) # supressing the warning










What makes observations with missing values different?
Example: nycflights13::flights, missing values in the dep_time variable indicate that the flight was cancelled. Want to compare scheduled departure times for cancelled and non-cancelled times. Can do this by making new variable, using ìs.na() to check if dep_timeis missing:

cancelled_flights <- nycflights13::flights |>
  mutate(
    cancelled = is.na(dep_time),
    sched_hour = sched_dep_time %/% 100, 
    sched_min = sched_dep_time %% 100,
    sched_dep_time = sched_hour + (sched_min / 60)
    )

ggplot(
  data = cancelled_flights,
  mapping = aes(x = sched_dep_time)) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(color = cancelled), binwidth = 1/4)







# Alternatively, can facet by cancelled flights, and set scales free

ggplot(
  data = cancelled_flights,
  mapping = aes(x = sched_dep_time)
) +
  geom_freqpoly(mapping = aes(color = cancelled), binwidth = 1/4) +
  facet_wrap(~cancelled, scale = "free") +
  scale_color_colorblind()







# Or, even better, see upcoming content, use after_stat()

ggplot(
  data = cancelled_flights,
  mapping = aes(x = sched_dep_time, y = after_stat(density))
) +
  geom_freqpoly(mapping = aes(color = cancelled), binwidth = 1/4)














Note



geom_freqpoly {ggplot2}: Visualise the distribution of a single continuous variable by dividing the x axis into bins and counting the number of observations in each bin. Histograms (geom_histogram()) display the counts with bars; frequency polygons (geom_freqpoly()) display the counts with lines.

title: Exploratory data analysis - EDA
text:
Covariation
Variation describing behavior within a variable; Covariation describing behavior between variables.
Covariation is the tendency for the values of two or more variables to vary together in a related way. Best way to spot covariation is by visualizing the relationship between two or more variables.

A categorical & numerical variable
Example: Comparing price of diamond vs. quality (cut) using geom_freqpoly():

# Left
ggplot(
  data = diamonds, 
  mapping = aes(x = price) 
) +
  geom_freqpoly(mapping = aes(color = cut), binwidth = 500, linewidth = 0.75) +   scale_color_colorblind()







# Right
ggplot(
  data = diamonds, 
  mapping = aes(x = price, y = after_stat(density)) 
# standardized now, instead of displaying count only, making comparison easier
# See ?geom_freqploy or ?stat_bin, the underlying mechanism of geom_freqpol()
) +
  geom_freqpoly(mapping = aes(color = cut), binwidth = 500, linewidth = 0.75) +   scale_color_colorblind()







# Simpler approach is side-by-side boxplots
ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = cut, y = price)) +
    geom_boxplot()














Tip



cutis ordered factor, BUT many categorcial variables dont have such intrinsic order, hence reordering is appropriate. Do so by fct_reorder()



# Example 1
ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = cut, y = price)
) + 
 geom_boxplot(
   mapping = aes(x = fct_reorder(cut, price, median)))







# Example 2
ggplot(
  data = mpg, 
  mapping = aes(x = fct_reorder(class, hwy, median), y = hwy)
) +
  geom_boxplot()







# Example 3: Flipping axis with long names
ggplot(
  data = mpg, 
  mapping = aes(y = fct_reorder(class, hwy, median), x = hwy)
) +
  geom_boxplot()







# Example 4: use coord_flip()
ggplot(
  data = mpg,
  mapping = aes(x = fct_reorder(class, hwy, median), y = hwy)
) + 
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip()










Miscellaneous






Note



One problem with boxplots is that they were developed in an era of much smaller datasets and tend to display a prohibitively large number of “outlying values”. One approach to remedy this problem is the letter value plot.



# Example of lvplot, refer to ?lvplot
# install.packages("lvplot")
library(lvplot)
?lvplot

ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = cut, y = price)
) + 
  geom_lv(mapping = aes(fill = after_stat(LV))) +
  scale_y_sqrt() +
  theme_bw()








There is also the option to display a relationship via geom_violin().

ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = fct_reorder(cut, price, median), y = price)
) + 
  geom_violin(quantile.linetype = 1L, quantile.color = "red")










Two categorical variables
To visualize covariation between two categorical variables, need to count the number of observations forch each combination of levels of these categorical variables.

# One way is via geom_count()
ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = cut, y = color)
) + 
  geom_count()














Note



Size of circles display how many observations occurred at each combination of values. Covariation will appear as a strong correlation.


Another approach:

diamonds |> 
  count(color, cut) |>
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x = color, y = cut)
  ) +
  geom_tile(
    mapping = aes(fill = n)
  )







# Alternatively: Distribution of cut within color
diamonds |> 
  count(color, cut) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n), .by = color) |>
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x = color, y = cut)
  ) +
  geom_tile(
    mapping = aes(fill = prop)
  )







# Alternatively: Distribution of color within cut
diamonds |> 
  count(color, cut) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n), .by = cut) |>
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x = color, y = cut)
  ) +
  geom_tile(
    mapping = aes(fill = prop)
  )














Tip



For unordered categorical variables use seriation package, for larger plots use heatmaply package.




Two numerical variables
Great way to visualize the covariation between two numerical variables: draw a scatterplot with geom_point().

ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(x = carat, y = price)
) +
  geom_point()







# Focusing on bulk of diamonds smaller than 3 carat
diamonds |> 
  filter(carat < 3) |>
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x = carat, y = price)
  ) + 
  geom_point()














Warning



Scatterplots become less useful when dataset grows, as points begin to overplot; can fix problem with alpha argument.



smaller <- diamonds |>
  filter(carat < 3)
# Inducing transparency
ggplot(
  data = smaller,
  mapping = aes(x = carat, y = price)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 1/100)








Alternatively, can use bins, i.e. geom_bin2d() and geom_hex(), to bin in two dimensions. Both divide coordinate plane into 2d bins and use fill color to display how many points fall into each bin.

geom_bin2d() creates rectangular bins.
geom_hex() creates hexagonal bins.


# Install package for geom_hex()
# install.packages("hexbin")

# Example geom_bin2d()
ggplot(
  data = smaller,
  mapping = aes(x = carat, y = price)
) + 
  geom_bin2d()







# Example geom_hex()
ggplot(
  data = smaller,
  mapping = aes(x = carat, y = price)
) +
  geom_hex()








Alternatively, bin one continuous variable, acting as categorical variable:

ggplot(
  data = smaller,
  mapping = aes(x = carat, y = price)
) + 
  geom_boxplot(
    mapping = aes(group = cut_width(carat, 0.1)), varwidth = TRUE
  )

Warning: Orientation is not uniquely specified when both the x and y aesthetics are
continuous. Picking default orientation 'x'.















Note



cut_with(x, width) divides x into bins of width width. varwidth = TRUE makes the width of boxplot proportional to number of points.




Miscellaneous
Instead summarizing conditional distribution with boxplots, could use frequency polygon:

ggplot(
  data = smaller,
  mapping = aes(x = price, color = cut_number(carat, 6))
) +
  geom_freqpoly()

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.

  data = smaller,
  mapping = aes(x = price, color = cut_width(carat, 0.2))
) +
  geom_freqpoly()

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.

title: Missing values
text:
Explicit missing values
Explicit values - i.e., cells with NA.

Last observation carried forward
Common use for missing values is as data entry convenience. Missing values, when entry by hand, indicate that previous value should be carried forward, i.e., repeated:

# Carrying forward values by NA values
treatment <- tribble(
  ~person, ~treatment, ~response,
  "Derrick Whitemore", 1, 7,
  NA, 2, 10, 
  NA, 3, NA, 
  "Katherine Burke", 1, 4
)

# treatment |>
#   fill(person, treatment, response)

treatment |>
  fill(everything())

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  person            treatment response
  <chr>                 <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Derrick Whitemore         1        7
2 Derrick Whitemore         2       10
3 Derrick Whitemore         3       10
4 Katherine Burke           1        4

# locf = "last observation carried forward"



Fixed values
Sometime NA represent fixed, known values, most commonly 0. Can use dplyr::coalesce():

x <- c(1, 4, 5, 7, NA)
coalesce(x, 0)

[1] 1 4 5 7 0

# Can specify NA values when reading in CSV data
# read_csv(file = path, na = "99"), specify all "99" values as NA

# Alternatively use na_if():
x <- c(1, 4, 5, 7, -99)
na_if(x, -99)

[1]  1  4  5  7 NA




NaN
Special type of NA value: NaN (not a number). Behaves like NA values:

x <- c(NA, NaN)
x * 10 

[1]  NA NaN

x == 1

[1] NA NA

is.na(x)

[1] TRUE TRUE

is.nan(x)

[1] FALSE  TRUE

na_if(c(TRUE, 99), x)

[1]  1 99


Encounter NaN when performing math:

0 / 0

[1] NaN

0 * Inf

[1] NaN

Inf - Inf

[1] NaN

sqrt(-1)

Warning in sqrt(-1): NaNs produced


[1] NaN

stocks <- tibble(

)


price in 4th quarter of 2020 - NA - explicit
price 1st quarter of 2021 - does not appear in dataset- implicit

text:
Factors and empty groups
Group not containing any observations - can arise when working with factors:

health <- tibble(
  name   = c("Ikaia", "Oletta", "Leriah", "Dashay", "Tresaun"),
  smoker = factor(c("no", "no", "no", "no", "no"), levels = c("yes", "no")),
  age    = c(34, 88, 75, 47, 56),
)

health |>
  count(smoker) # smoker groups is empty, but we know they exist

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  smoker     n
  <fct>  <int>
1 no         5

levels(health$smoker)

[1] "yes" "no"

  count(smoker, .drop = FALSE) # now count for smoker is included

# A tibble: 2 × 2

  <fct>  <int>
1 yes        0
2 no         5

ggplot(health, aes(x = smoker)) +

  scale_x_discrete()







ggplot(health, aes(x = smoker)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE)

Regular expressions

Key functions
str_detect() returns logical vector - TRUE pattern matches element or character vector, FALSE otherwise. Pairs well with filter() and summarize():

title: Regular expressions
text:
Pattern details

Escaping
Matching matcharacters, like ., requires escaping. Regexps use backslash for escaping - so need to \. - BUT \ also special character, thus \\. is required.

dot <- "\\."

str_view(dot)

[1] │ \.

str_view(c("abc", "a.c", "bef"), pattern = "\\.")

[2] │ a<.>c

str_view(c("abc", "a.c", "bef"), pattern = "a\\.c")

[2] │ <a.c>

# To match literal \ need "\\\\"

x <- "a\\b"

str_view(x)

[1] │ a\b

str_view(x, pattern = "\\\\")

[1] │ a<\>b

# Can use raw strings alternatively:

str_view(x, pattern = r"{\\}")

[1] │ a<\>b

# Matching literal ., $, |, *, +, ?, {, }, (, ) via []:

str_view(c("abc", "a.b", "a*c", "a c"), pattern = "[.]")

[2] │ a<.>b

str_view(c("abc", "a.b", "a*c", "a c"), pattern = "[*]c")

[3] │ a<*c>




Anchors
Use anchors to match at start or end of string - use ^ for start, use $ for end.

str_view(fruit, pattern = "^a")

[1] │ <a>pple
[2] │ <a>pricot
[3] │ <a>vocado

str_view(fruit, pattern = "a$")

 [4] │ banan<a>
[15] │ cherimoy<a>
[30] │ feijo<a>
[36] │ guav<a>
[56] │ papay<a>
[74] │ satsum<a>

str_view(fruit, pattern = "^apple$")

[1] │ <apple>


Can also match boundaries between words:

x <- c("summary(x)", "summarize(df)", "rowsum(x)", "sum(x)")

str_view(x, pattern = "sum")

[1] │ <sum>mary(x)
[2] │ <sum>marize(df)
[3] │ row<sum>(x)
[4] │ <sum>(x)

str_view(x, pattern = "\\bsum\\b")

[4] │ <sum>(x)

# produce alone a zero-width match
str_view("abc", pattern = c("^", "$", "\\b"))

[1] │ <>abc
[2] │ abc<>
[3] │ <>abc<>

str_replace_all("abc", pattern = c("^", "$", "\\b"), replacement = "__")

[1] "__abc"   "abc__"   "__abc__"




Character classes
Character class, character set - allows matching any character in a set. Can construct sets via []: + [^abc]: Matches any character except “a”, “b”, “c”. + [a-z]: matches any lower case letter + [0-9]: matches any number + \: escapes special characters, e.g., [^-]] matches ^, -, ]

x <- "abc ABCD 12345 -!@#%."

str_view(x, pattern = "[abc]")

[1] │ <a><b><c> ABCD 12345 -!@#%.

str_view(x, pattern = "[a-z]")

[1] │ <a><b><c> ABCD 12345 -!@#%.

str_view(x, pattern = "[abc]+")

[1] │ <abc> ABCD 12345 -!@#%.

str_view(x, pattern = "[^a-z0-9]+")

[1] │ abc< ABCD >12345< -!@#%.>

# You need an escape to match characters that are special inside []
str_view("a-b-c", pattern = "[a-c]")

[1] │ <a>-<b>-<c>

str_view("a-b-c", pattern = "[a\\-c]")

[1] │ <a><->b<-><c>

str_view(x, pattern = "\\w+")

[1] │ <abc> <ABCD> <12345> -!@#%.

str_view(x, pattern = "\\d+")

[1] │ abc ABCD <12345> -!@#%.


Shortcut: + \d: matches any digit + \D: matches anything other than digit + \s: matches whitespace + \S: matches anything other than whitespace + \w: matches any “word” character + \W: matches any “non-word” character


Quantifiers
Control how many times pattern matches: + ?: 0 or 1 matches + +: 1 or more matches + *: 0 or more matches + {n}: matches exactly n times + {n,}: matches at least n times + {n,m}: matches between n and m times


Operator precedence and parentheses
Quantifiers have high precedence and alternation has low precedence which means that ab+ is equivalent to a(b+), and ^a|b$ is equivalent to (^a)|(b$). Just like with algebra, you can use parentheses to override the usual order.


Grouping and capturing
Capturing groups allowing to use sub-components of the match via back reference: \1 refers to match contained in first parenthesis, \2 in the second parenthesis, and so on.

# Finding repeated pair of letters
str_view(fruit, pattern = "(..)\\1")

 [4] │ b<anan>a
[20] │ <coco>nut
[22] │ <cucu>mber
[41] │ <juju>be
[56] │ <papa>ya
[73] │ s<alal> berry

# Finding word starting and ending with same pair of letters
str_view(words, pattern = "^(..).*\\1$")

[152] │ <church>
[217] │ <decide>
[617] │ <photograph>
[699] │ <require>
[739] │ <sense>

Regex flags
Settings to control details of regexp - called flags - i.e., wrapping pattern in a call to regex(). Most useful flag is ìgnore_case = TRUE - allowing matching upper- or lowercase forms:

bananas <- c("banana", "Banana", "BANANA")
str_view(bananas)

[1] │ banana
[2] │ Banana
[3] │ BANANA

str_view(bananas, pattern = regex("banana", ignore_case = TRUE))

[1] │ <banana>
[2] │ <Banana>
[3] │ <BANANA>



dotall = TRUE lets . match everything including \n:


x <- "Line 1\nLine 2\nLine 3"

str_view(x)

[1] │ Line 1
    │ Line 2
    │ Line 3

str_view(x, pattern = ".Line")

✖ Empty `string` provided.

str_view(x, pattern = regex(pattern = ".Line", dotall = TRUE))

[1] │ Line 1<
    │ Line> 2<
    │ Line> 3



multiline = TRUE makes ^ and $ match start and end of each line rather than start and end of complete string:


x <- "Line 1\nLine 2\nLine 3"
str_view(x, "^Line")

    │ Line 2
    │ Line 3

str_view(x, regex("^Line", multiline = TRUE))

[1] │ <Line> 1
    │ <Line> 2

Caution



Factors are used for categorical variables - known set of possible values.
Also useful when displaying character vectors in non-alphabetical order.

title: factors
text:
Factor basics

x1 <- c("Dec", "Apr", "Jan", "Mar")

# Issues: Only twelve possible months and danger of typos; doesn't sort in useful way

x2 <- c("Dec", "Apr", "Jam", "Mar")
sort(x1)

[1] "Apr" "Dec" "Jan" "Mar"

# Solution: Factors
# create list of valid levels

month_levels <- c(
  "Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
  "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"
)


# Specifiying Levels
y <- factor(x = x1) # omitting levels results in levels being taken from data in alphabetical order
y

[1] Dec Apr Jan Mar
Levels: Apr Dec Jan Mar

sort(y)

[1] Apr Dec Jan Mar
Levels: Apr Dec Jan Mar

# Not specifying levels
y1 <- factor(x = x1, levels = month_levels) 
y1

[1] Dec Apr Jan Mar
Levels: Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec

sort(y1) # with levels added, can ensure correct alphabetical order

[1] Jan Mar Apr Dec
Levels: Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec



# What happens to typos after adding levels?
y2 <- factor(x = x2, levels = month_levels)
y2 # can see that typo will be spottet by predefining levels

[1] Dec  Apr  <NA> Mar 
Levels: Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec

sort(y2) # NA will be omitted in sorting

[1] Mar Apr Dec
Levels: Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec



# Can use forcats::fct() - will not convert faulty values silently to NA
# y3 <- fct(x2, levels = month_levels)

# forcats::fct orders by first appearance:
fct(x1)

[1] Dec Apr Jan Mar
Levels: Dec Apr Jan Mar

# Can access levels via levels():
levels(y2)

 [1] "Jan" "Feb" "Mar" "Apr" "May" "Jun" "Jul" "Aug" "Sep" "Oct" "Nov" "Dec"

csv <- c("

ordered(c("a", "b", "c"))

Different behavior in two places, compared to regular factors: + mapping ordered factor to color in ggplot2 defaults to scale_color_viridis() - color scale implying ranking + in linear models, when using ordered predictor, will use “polynomial contrasts”.
